questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about explicit mentalizing is true?

options.text: Explicit mentalizing is like narrative.
Explicit mentalizing prohibits learning from past mistakes in order to interact more effectively in the future.
Explicit mentalizing takes others' knowledge and emotional states automatically into account.
Explicit mentalizing is used primarily when encountering familiar situations.
Explicit mentalizing is uncontrolled and unconscious.

questions.explanation: Explicit mentalizing is relatively controlled, predominantly taking the form of narrative; people routinely tell stories to others and themselves about their mental states, the reasons for them, and their history. These stories are more or less elaborate, ranging from simply putting feelings into words to creating more complex autobiographical narratives. Explicit mentalizing, like consciousness more generally, permits mental time travel: people mentalize not only about the present (e.g., exploring reasons for current feelings) but also about the past (e.g., reconstructing the basis for a prior interpersonal conflict or impulsive action) and the future (e.g., anticipating the best way to address a relationship challenge). In contrast, implicit mentalizing is relatively automatic, procedural, and nonconscious, such as in turn-taking in conversation, adapting voice tone and posture to others’ emotional states, and taking others’ knowledge into account automatically (e.g., not referring to Jane when the other person has no idea who Jane is).

questions.question_text: Relying on cognition without any insight into real emotional meaning is an example of extreme imbalance in which of the following types of mentalizing?

options.text: Implicit mentalizing.
Affective mentalizing.
External mentalizing.
Cognitive mentalizing.
Internal mentalizing.

questions.explanation: The focus in cognitive mentalizing is thoughts and beliefs; that in affective mentalizing is emotions and feelings. Extreme imbalance in either direction poses challenges for psychotherapy. For example, patients with an overreliance on cognition might be adept at generating explicit reasons for their own or others’ behavior, but such insight—devoid of any real emotional meaning—does not promote change. Conversely, patients who are more prone to being flooded with affect are employing implicit processes conducive to emotional contagion and impaired self-other differentiation. For patients at both ends of this spectrum, mentalizing emotion—thinking and feeling about thinking and feeling—is a crucial therapeutic goal. External mentalizing entails responsiveness to external, observable aspects of behavior—most prominently facial expressions, but also voice tone and posture. In contrast, internal mentalizing requires inference and imagination in the service of understanding the mental states conjoined with external behavior (i.e., desires, feelings, beliefs, and relationship proclivities).

questions.question_text: Skillful mentalizing is a goal of psychotherapy that is best characterized by which of the following?

options.text: Mentalizing with complete accuracy.
Mentalizing with benevolent intent.
Attempting to hide authentic emotion so as not to overwhelm the other person.
Maintaining focus on self at all times.
Linking external behavior with mental states.

questions.explanation: Hallmarks of skillful mentalizing include mentalizing with reasonable accuracy, mentalizing with benevolent intent, grounding mentalizing in authentic emotion, and flexibly integrating the multiple facets of mentalizing. Options A, C, D, and E are not aspects of skillful mentalizing.

questions.question_text: The experience of feeling 'thought about' creates which of the following?

options.text: The sense of safety needed to explore the social world.
A disrupted capacity for social learning.
Protection from attachment trauma.
Disorganized attachment with impaired mentalizing capacity.
The expectation that others will always treat us well.

correct_answer.text: The sense of safety needed to explore the social world.

correct_answers.text: The sense of safety needed to explore the social world.

questions.explanation: As Bowlby (1988) asserted in the context of psychotherapy, security in attachment relationships is conducive to exploring one’s own and others’ mental states. In sum, the experience of feeling thought about promotes the sense of safety needed to think and learn about the social world in interactions with others throughout life. Our feeling that the other person can see the world from our perspective (i.e., when they mentalize us) is the basis for epistemic trust and opens up our wish to learn about the world. The attachment system serves the evolutionary function of establishing general epistemic trust in the social world by producing an expectation that others will respond to us in a sensitively responsive and psychologically attuned way—that is, enabling us to feel that we are known.

questions.question_text: Dissociative symptoms have been associated with which of the following?

options.text: Secure attachment.
High IQ scores.
Bed wetting.
The ability to understand what others are feeling.
Attachment trauma.

questions.explanation: Attachment trauma engenders an aversion to mentalizing insofar as awareness of the parent’s fear, hatred, sadism, or indifference is extremely painful and threatening by virtue of leaving the child in danger and without protection. Attachment trauma and disorganization have been shown to relate to developmental psychopathology from childhood (Carlson et al. 2009) to adulthood (Lyons-Ruth and Jacobvitz 2008). Although childhood attachment trauma is best regarded as a nonspecific risk factor for a wide array of later psychopathology, there is one exception: infant disorganization, which includes dissociative behavior, is associated with dissociative symptoms in childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood (Carlson 1998).

questions.question_text: Reflective functioning, a concept closely related to mentalizing, has been associated with which of the following?

options.text: Empathy with the feelings of others.
A strong observing ego.
The capacity for insight.
Marked social intelligence.
A strong ability to narrate childhood attachment relationships.

correct_answer.text: A strong ability to narrate childhood attachment relationships.

correct_answers.text: A strong ability to narrate childhood attachment relationships.

questions.explanation: Given that mentalizing is fundamental to human relationships— relating to oneself as well as relating to others—it is little wonder that mentalizing overlaps in various ways with many cognate concepts, including empathy, psychological mindedness, observing ego, insight, theory of mind, mind reading, social cognition, metacognition, social intelligence, and emotional intelligence. The term reflective functioning bears especially close kinship to mentalizing in being a well-established measure of mentalizing capacity (Fonagy et al. 1998), based on assessments of the arena in which mentalizing is most challenging—namely, narratives regarding childhood attachment relationships, a common component of psychotherapeutic discourse.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the skill set of successful mentalizing?

options.text: Flexibly integrating the multiple facets of mentalizing.
Balancing focus on self and others.
Linking external behavior with internal mental states.
Integrating cognitive and affective mentalizing.
All of the above.

questions.explanation: To a great degree, skillful mentalizing entails flexible integration of the multiple facets of mentalizing: balancing focus on self and others; integrating cognitive and affective mentalizing; being able to link external behavior with internal mental states; and relying on implicit and intuitive mentalizing while employing explicit and reflective mentalizing when confronting problems or engaging in more complex interactions (e.g., in challenging negotiations or psychotherapy).

questions.question_text: In mentalization-based therapy, if the therapist fails to grasp the patient's experience with reasonable accuracy, which of the following is likely to occur?

options.text: The therapeutic alliance will be permanently ruptured.
The therapeutic alliance may be preserved if the therapist exemplifies openness and responsiveness to the patient's point of view.
The therapeutic alliance may be preserved if the therapist apologizes to the patient repeatedly.
The therapist will conclude that the patient is not ready for mentalization-based therapy.
The therapist will conclude that the patient is not being transparent enough, and this must be pointed out.

correct_answer.text: The therapeutic alliance may be preserved if the therapist exemplifies openness and responsiveness to the patient's point of view.

correct_answers.text: The therapeutic alliance may be preserved if the therapist exemplifies openness and responsiveness to the patient's point of view.

questions.explanation: Continuous and perfect alignment of perspectives would not promote learning; therapy invariably entails a fluid process of alignment, misalignment, and realignment of perspectives. The therapist must grasp the patient’s experience with reasonable accuracy much of the time while also challenging the patient’s perspective by bringing in another point of view. Moreover, the therapist also must exemplify openness and flexibility by responsiveness to the patient’s point of view, for example, when inevitably the therapist’s comments will be off the mark. This approach requires a high degree of transparency on the part of the therapist, which serves as a model of transparency for the patient—being able to speak directly and forthrightly about the experience of the relationship.

questions.question_text: Which of the following findings has been demonstrated in the Ainsworth's Strange Situation paradigm?

options.text: Securely attached infants seek contact and comfort from their mother upon reunion, and then, reassured, return to play.
Attachment is not related to learning.
A mother's mentalizing capacity is not predictive of her infant's attachment security.
Infants who are less securely attached develop greater abilities to mentalize in childhood.
Securely attached infants do not seek contact and comfort from their mothers upon reunion.

correct_answer.text: Securely attached infants seek contact and comfort from their mother upon reunion, and then, reassured, return to play.

correct_answers.text: Securely attached infants seek contact and comfort from their mother upon reunion, and then, reassured, return to play.

questions.explanation: To examine the relationship between parental mentalizing and subsequent infant attachment security, Fonagy et al. (1991) employed Ainsworth’s Strange Situation (Ainsworth et al. 1978), which entails moderately stressful parent-child separations and reunions in a playroom. In short, securely attached infants are more or less distressed by the separation; regardless, at the point of reunion, they seek contact and comfort from their mother and then, reassured, they return to play. Mothers’ mentalizing capacity in relation to their own attachment history predicted their infants’ attachment security in relation Mentalizing in relation to them (Fonagy et al. 1991). These findings generalized to fathers (Steele et al. 1996). Trauma in attachment relationships contributes to the intergenerational transmission of impaired mentalizing capacities (Fonagy et al. 2007)

questions.question_text: Disorganized attachment in infants is related not only to abuse and neglect but also to which of the following?

options.text: Low parental socioeconomic status and/or education.
High family levels of expressed emotion.
Parental poor health.
Disturbance of emotional communication in parent-infant interactions.
Lack of parental social supports.

correct_answer.text: Disturbance of emotional communication in parent-infant interactions.

correct_answers.text: Disturbance of emotional communication in parent-infant interactions.

questions.explanation: Infant attachment disorganization, the converse of secure attachment, is associated with impaired mentalizing capacities in childhood, a fundamentally problematic legacy of attachment trauma. Disorganized attachment in infants was first discovered to occur in relation to frank maltreatment (Main and Solomon 1990). Subsequent research has revealed more subtle disturbances in parents’ attachment discourse and parent-child interactions that are associated with disorganized attachment. That is, infant disorganization relates not only to parents’ trauma-related lapses (including dissociative states) in attachment interviews but also to more pervasive indications of hostile or helpless states of mind throughout the interviews (Melnick et al. 2008). In addition, infant disorganization is associated not only with frank maltreatment— abuse and neglect—but also with more pervasive disturbance of emotional communication in parent-infant interactions (Lyons-Ruth and Jacobvitz 2008) and a more general disabled caregiving system (George and Solomon 2011).

questions.question_text: Mentalization-based treatment (MBT) was originally developed for the treatment of which of the following conditions?

options.text: Borderline personality disorder.
Major depressive disorder.
Anxiety disorders.
Substance dependence.
Psychotic disorders.

questions.explanation: Although potentially useful in the other forms of psychopathology listed, MBT was originally developed for the treatment of borderline personality disorder (BPD). The core symptoms of BPD—emotional dysregulation, impulsivity, self-destructive behavior, and unstable relationships—are embedded in highly insecure (i.e., preoccupied and disorganized) attachment relationships and severe mentalizing impairments. More specifically, patients with BPD show marked impairments in the explicit, internal, and cognitive facets of mentalizing: they are reactive to external-behavioral cues (e.g., a grimace or a yawn), they have difficulty linking such cues appropriately to internal mental states, and they are subject to implicit mentalizing and emotional contagion concomitant with impaired capacity for explicit, reflective thinking (Fonagy and Luyten 2009).

questions.question_text: "Attentiveness to thinking and feeling in self and others" defines which of the following terms?

options.text: Transference.
Countertransference.
Mentalizing.
Psychological mindedness.
Mindfulness.

questions.explanation: In plain language, mentalizing can be characterized as attentiveness to thinking and feeling in self and others—or, in shorthand, as holding mind in mind. Mentalizing is technically defined as the natural human imaginative capacity to perceive and interpret behavior in self and others as conjoined with intentional mental states, such as desires, motives, feelings, and beliefs. Transference and countertransference are core psychodynamic principles that are not related to the question stem. Psychological mindedness relates to an individual’s capacity for introspection and self-examination. Mindfulness relates to present-centered attention.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements accurately characterizes mentalization-based treatment (MBT)?

options.text: MBT is used exclusively in the treatment of borderline personality disorder.
MBT can address deficits in social cognition that occur in multiple psychiatric disorders.
MBT is effective only in addressing certain forms of developmental psychopathology.
MBT is an effective treatment for bipolar and related disorders.
MBT is an effective treatment for autism spectrum disorder.

correct_answer.text: MBT can address deficits in social cognition that occur in multiple psychiatric disorders.

correct_answers.text: MBT can address deficits in social cognition that occur in multiple psychiatric disorders.

questions.explanation: Although MBT was developed to ameliorate deficits in social cognition commonly associated with borderline personality disorder, such deficits are evident in an array of psychiatric disorders for which mentalizing approaches are being developed, including substance abuse, eating disorders, depression, trauma, and other personality disorders.
